KAM tori for the generalized Bejamin-Bona-Mahony equation

Guanghua Shi, Dongfeng Yan Note: Corresponding author. Email:yand11@fudan.edu.cn Affiliation:  College of Mathematics and Statistics, Hunan Normal University,Changsha, Hunan 410006, China Affiliation:  School of Mathematics and Statistics, Zhengzhou University,Zhengzhou, Henan, 450001, China
Abstract

A generalized Benjamin-Bona-Mahony (gBBM) equation

ut−ux​x​t+ux+u4​ux=0,\displaystyle u_{t}-u_{xxt}+u_{x}+u^{4}u_{x}=0,

subject to the periodic boundary condition is studied in this paper. Based on a new infinite dimensional Kolomogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) theorem with normal frequencies of finite limit-points, it is shown that the gBBM equation admits plenty of time-quasi-periodic solutions with two frequencies of high modes.

Key words: gBBM equation; quasi-periodic solutions; KAM theorem.

1 Introduction and main result

The Benjamin-Bona-Mahony (BBM) equation

ut−ux​x​t+ux+u​ux=0,\displaystyle u_{t}-u_{xxt}+u_{x}+uu_{x}=0, (1)

which is also known as the regularized long-wave equation (RLWE), is initially proposed by Benjamin, Bona and Mahony in 1972 as an improvement of the KdV equation for modeling the long gravity waves of small amplitude in nonlinear dispersive systems [1]. In [1], Benjamin and his partners established the existence and uniqueness of the global solutions to the intial value problem of the BBM equation. The existence and uniqueness of the periodic solutions for the BBM equation is studied in [2]. Besides, it is worthwhile to mention that the BBM equation admits only three conservation laws [3], while the KdV equation possesses infinite conservation laws. Subsequently, many research work for the BBM equation were conducted. For instance, the global existence of the BBM equation in arbitrary dimension was established in Ref. [4], while the long time dynamics of the BBM equation was investigated in Ref. [5].

We mention that none of the aforementioned papers study the time-quasi-periodic solutions for the BBM equation, in consideration of this, Yuan initially establishes the time-quasi-periodic solutions for the BBM equation (1) based on his new infinite dimensional KAM theorem with normal frequencies of finite limit-points [6]. We shall briefly recall the history of the applications of the KAM theory into partial differential equations (PDEs), the key idea of which is to transform the PDEs into an infinite dimensional Hamiltonian system, then the Hamiltonian system is brought into a normal form with an invariant torus by generating iteratively a sequence of symplectic transformations. The pioneering work to study the PDEs in the frame of KAM theory were carried out by Kuksin [7, 8, 9, 10] and Wayne [11], see also Pöschel [12]. These aforemetioned papers concerned with the PDEs of spatial dimension d=1,d=1, for the case when the spatial dimension d≥2,d\geq 2, Bourgain [13, 14, 15, 16, 17] managed to develope a new theory which is based on the Newton iteration, Fröhlich-Spencer technique and the semi-algebraic set to study the KAM tori for the PDEs in high spatial dimension, see also Eliasson-Kuksin [18] and Eliasson-Grebert-Kuksin [19]. The existence of KAM tori and quasi-periodic solutions for PDEs with unbounded nonlinearities was developed by Kuksin [20] for the KdV equation (see also [21]). Later on, based on the improvement of the Kuksin’s Lemma (see [21]), Liu-Yuan [22, 23] extended the unbounded KAM theorem to the limiting case, and established the existence of the quasi-periodic solutions for the derivative nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the Benjamin-Ono equation. Recently, the existence of the quasi-peridic solutions for the quasi-linear PDEs was studied in [24, 25, 26].

It should be pointed out that one of the underlying assumptions of the aforementioned KAM theorem is that the normal frequencies λj\lambda_{j}’s in the normal form part always cluster to infinity. To be specific, there exists some κ≥1\kappa\geq 1 fulfilling

λj≈|j|κ→∞,as|j|→∞.\lambda_{j}\approx|j|^{\kappa}\to\infty,\quad\text{as}\quad|j|\to\infty.

For example, when one considers the nonlinear Schrödinger equation

i​ut−ux​x+m​u+u3=0,u⁡(x,0)=u⁡(x,2​π)=0,\displaystyle iu_{t}-u_{xx}+mu+u^{3}=0,\quad u(x,0)=u(x,2\pi)=0, (2)

where m>0m>0 is a constant, its normal frequencies take the form λj=j2+m≈j2\lambda_{j}=j^{2}+m\approx j^{2}. It is well known that when one constructs the lower dimensional KAM tori, he has to make sure that the first Melnikov’s conditions always hold ture, that is,

Δk​j=⟨k,ω⟩+λj≠0,∀(k,j)∈ℤN+1,\Delta_{kj}=\langle k,\omega\rangle+\lambda_{j}\neq 0,\forall(k,j)\in\mathbb{Z}^{N+1},

in which ω\omega represents the tangential frequency of the integrable normal form part. By the analyticity of the perturbation term, one could impose some restriction on kk, say,

|k|≤K=Kν≈2ν,|k|\leq K=K_{\nu}\approx 2^{\nu},

in which ν\nu represents the step number of the KAM iteration. Specially, when |j|>C​K|j|>CK with CC larger enough than the norm of the tangential frequency |ω||\omega|, one has

|Δk​j|>|λj|−|k|​|ω|>|j|2−|ω|K>1,|\Delta_{kj}|>|\lambda_{j}|-|k||\omega|>|j|^{2}-|\omega|K>1,

which simply indicates that the number of the small divisor Δk​j\Delta_{kj} is finite in the first Melnikov’s conditions. However, when one turns to consider the BBM equation, the normal frequency takes the following form

λj=j1+j2→0,asj→∞,\lambda_{j}=\frac{j}{1+j^{2}}\to 0,\quad\text{as}\quad j\to\infty,

which means the number of the small divisors Δk​j\Delta_{kj} is infinite in the first Melnikov’s conditions. This is a huge difference between the former KAM theorems and Yuan’s KAM theorem with normal frequencies clustering to finite point [6].

This paper is concerned with the generalized Benjamin-Bona-Mahony (gBBM) equation subject to the periodic boundary condition

ut−ux​x​t+ux+u4​ux=0,u⁡(t,0)=u⁡(t,2​π).\displaystyle u_{t}-u_{xxt}+u_{x}+u^{4}u_{x}=0,\quad u(t,0)=u(t,2\pi). (3)

We mention that the decay property and the long-time behavior of the solutions for the generalized BBM equation were investigated in [28, 29, 30, 31]. The aim of this paper is to study the quasi-periodic solutions for the gBBM equation (3) by means of the KAM method.

Due to the new infinite dimensional KAM theorem in [6], our main result of the present paper is presented below.

Theorem 1.1.

For given 1≪n1≪n2,1\ll n_{1}\ll n_{2}, in the neighborhood of the zero solution u=0u=0, the gBBM equation (3) admits plenty of smooth solutions which are quasi-periodic in time, linear stable and of zero Lyapunov exponent. More precisely, there exists ϵ∗=ϵ∗​(n1,n2)>0\epsilon^{*}=\epsilon^{*}(n_{1},n_{2})>0 such that, for any ϵ∈(0,ϵ∗)\epsilon\in(0,\epsilon^{*}), there is a subset 𝒪~\tilde{\mathcal{O}} of the initial value set 𝒪∗:=[ϵ12,4​ϵ12]2\mathcal{O}_{*}:=[\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}},4\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}]^{2} with

Leb​𝒪~=Leb​𝒪∗⋅(1−C​1|ln⁡ϵ|)\text{Leb}{\tilde{\mathcal{O}}}=\text{Leb}\mathcal{O}_{*}\cdot(1-C\frac{1}{|\ln\epsilon|})

and for each ξ∈𝒪~\xi\in\tilde{\mathcal{O}}, the gBBM equation (3) possesses a quasi-periodic solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) of frequency ω∈ℝ2\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{2} in time t, that is,

u⁡(t,x)=∑k∈ℤ2,j∈ℤ∖{0}u^​(k,j)​ei⁡(k,ω)​t​ei​j​xu(t,x)=\sum\limits_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^{2},j\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}}\hat{u}(k,j)e^{i(k,\omega)t}e^{ijx}

fulfilling

|ω−ω0|≤Cϵ12,ω0=(n11+n12,n21+n22),|u^​(el,nl)−ξl|<Cϵ58,l=1,2,\displaystyle\begin{split}|\omega-\omega_{0}|&\leq C\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}},\quad\omega_{0}=(\frac{n_{1}}{1+n_{1}^{2}},\frac{n_{2}}{1+n_{2}^{2}}),\\ |\hat{u}(e_{l},n_{l})-\xi_{l}|&<C\epsilon^{\frac{5}{8}},\quad l=1,2,\\ \end{split}

and

∑(k,j)∉𝓆|u^(k,j)|2e|k|​s0+2​a​|j||j|2​p<Cϵ58,𝓆=(el,nl),l=1,2,\sum\limits_{(k,j)\not\in\mathcal{q}}|\hat{u}(k,j)|^{2}e^{|k|s_{0}+2a|j|}|j|^{2p}<C\epsilon^{\frac{5}{8}},\quad\mathcal{q}=(e_{l},n_{l}),l=1,2,

where ele_{l} denotes the l−l-th unit vector of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, and s0>0s_{0}>0, a>0a>0, p>12p>\frac{1}{2} are some constants.

Remark 1.2.

In the Section 9 of [6], Yuan derives the existence of the NN-dimensional KAM tori thus quasi-periodic solutions for the BBM equation (1) subject to the periodic boundary condition based on an additional assumption. More precisely, if the spatial varialbe x lies in a closed internal [0,A][0,A], then 2​πA\frac{2\pi}{A} is supposed to be a transcendental number, which is necessary to ensure that the combinations of the frequencies do not vanish and the initial Hamiltonian function can be transformed into the required partial Birkhoff normal form. In the present paper, we try to drop this assumption, that is, we choose the period to be the ordinary one, say, A=2​πA=2\pi. By choosing suitable admissable set and conducting the partial Birkhoff normal of order 14, we truely obtain the time-quasi-periodic solutions for the gBBM equation (3) with two frequencies of high modes. Unfortunately, we fail to obtain the NN-dimensional KAM tori and corresponding quasi-periodic solutions.

Remark 1.3.

It should be pointed out that the combinations of the frequencies vanish in many situations when we consider the case A=2​πA=2\pi, say, if (j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6)=(1,−2,−2,3,n,−n)(j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6})=(1,-2,-2,3,n,-n), then λj1+λj2+λj3+λj4+λj5+λj6=0.\lambda_{j_{1}}+\lambda_{j_{2}}+\lambda_{j_{3}}+\lambda_{j_{4}}+\lambda_{j_{5}}+\lambda_{j_{6}}=0. So we can not remove the nonresonant terms z1​z−2​z−2​z3​zn​z−nz_{1}z_{-2}z_{-2}z_{3}z_{n}z_{-n} when deriving the Birkhoff normal form. This is the reason why we have to choose some special high modes as the tangential frequencies.

Let us make some comments. To apply the KAM theorem developed by [6], we firstly turn the gBBM equation (3) into an infinite dimensional Hamiltonian system (7), (8) and (9). Note that the eigenvalue λj\lambda_{j} converges to zero, not +∞+\infty, which is very different from that of the classical KAM theory. It is worthwhile to point out that since the gBBM equation (3) does not contain any external parameters, it requires to extract the internal parameters ξ\xi from the partial Birkhoff normal form to apply the KAM theorem. To be more specific, we choose {z±n1,z±n2}\{z_{\pm n_{1}},z_{\pm n_{2}}\} as the suitable tangential variables, and the others {zj}j≠±n1,±n2\{z_{j}\}_{j\neq\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}} as the normal ones. It requires to remove those terms with (j1,j2,⋯,j6)∈(Δ0∪Δ1∪Δ2)∖𝒩(j_{1},j_{2},\cdots,j_{6})\in(\Delta_{0}\cup\Delta_{1}\cup\Delta_{2})\setminus\mathcal{N} through a symplectic transformation to obtain the partial Birkhoff normal form of order 6 (for the precise definitions of Δ0,\Delta_{0},Δ1\Delta_{1},Δ2\Delta_{2} and 𝒩\mathcal{N}, see Section 3). However, the perturbation term P=G^+RP=\hat{G}+R in the new Hamiltonian (24) fails to satisfy the Assumption C of the KAM theorem in [6], where the size of the Hamiltonian vector field XPX_{P} is assumed to be ϵ\epsilon and the size of ∂ξXP\partial_{\xi}X_{P} is assumed to be ϵ12\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}.

We shall make some explanations. Roughly speaking, the perturbation terms satisfy (see Proposition 3.2)

R=O⁡(‖z‖10),G^=O⁡(‖z‖3​‖z^‖3),\displaystyle R=O(\|z\|^{10}),\quad\hat{G}=O(\|z\|^{3}\|\hat{z}\|^{3}),

where z^=(zj)j∈ℕ∖{n1,n2}.\hat{z}=(z_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{n_{1},n_{2}\}}. Assume that ‖z‖=O⁡(ϵ18)\|z\|=O(\epsilon^{\frac{1}{8}}) and ‖z^‖=O⁡(ϵb)\|\hat{z}\|=O(\epsilon^{b}) with b>14b>\frac{1}{4}, then the parameters ξ\xi defined by (4) are of O⁡(ϵ12)O(\epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}), and the estimations of the corresponding Hamiltonian vector field are given by

‖XG^‖=O⁡(ϵ38+b),‖XR‖=O⁡(ϵ54−2​b).\displaystyle\|X_{\hat{G}}\|=O(\epsilon^{\frac{3}{8}+b}),\quad\|X_{R}\|=O(\epsilon^{\frac{5}{4}-2b}).

Since b>14b>\frac{1}{4}, the size of ‖XR‖\|X_{R}\| is larger than ϵ.\epsilon. Therefore, we have to remove some ”bad” terms of order 10 with (j1,⋯,j10)∈(Δ0′∪Δ1′)∖𝒩′(j_{1},\cdots,j_{10})\in(\Delta_{0}^{\prime}\cup\Delta_{1}^{\prime})\setminus\mathcal{N}^{\prime} in RR (the definitions of Δ0′\Delta_{0}^{\prime},Δ1′\Delta_{1}^{\prime},𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} are given in Section 3). By contrast, in [32], the authors only need to eliminate the terms of order 10 with (j1,⋯,j10)∈Δ0′∖𝒩′(j_{1},\cdots,j_{10})\in\Delta_{0}^{\prime}\setminus\mathcal{N}^{\prime}, which is sufficient to check the KAM theorem developed by [12]. By the same procedure, one obtains the partial Birkhoff normal form of order 10 in Proposition 3.4, in view of (42) and (43), we have

‖XR^‖=O⁡(ϵ),‖XT‖=O⁡(ϵ74−2​b)\displaystyle\|X_{\hat{R}}\|=O(\epsilon),\quad\|X_{T}\|=O(\epsilon^{\frac{7}{4}-2b})

If we expect the size of XTX_{T} to be less than ϵ\epsilon, then one has to impose an restriction on bb, that is, 74−2​b≥1,\frac{7}{4}-2b\geq 1, i.e., b≤38b\leq\frac{3}{8}. Unfortunately, under this circumstance, the size of the vector field XG^X_{\hat{G}} is still larger than ϵ,\epsilon, which determines that one still needs to eliminate the relative large term in TT of order 14 with (j1,⋯,j14)∈Δ0′′∖𝒩′′(j_{1},\cdots,j_{14})\in\Delta_{0}^{\prime\prime}\setminus\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} (the precise definitions of Δ0′′\Delta_{0}^{\prime\prime} and 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} are presented in Section 3). Luckily, we remark that the perturbation term appears in the new partial Birkhoff normal form of order 14 fulfills all the assumptions of the KAM theorem in [6], see Propostion 3.6. Moreover, it is worth mentioning that in the above procedures, one has to guarantee the small divisors |λj1+⋯+λjl|​(l=6,10,14)|\lambda_{j_{1}}+\cdots+\lambda_{j_{l}}|(l=6,10,14) do not vanish when (j1,⋯,jl)(j_{1},\cdots,j_{l}) belongs to some admissible index sets, see Proposition 3.1, Lemma 3.3 and Lemma 3.5.

2 The Hamiltonian

After equipped with the symplectic structure −(1−∂x​x)−1∂x-(1-\partial_{xx})^{-1}\partial_{x} and the model space

u∈ℋ0p0:={u∈ℋp0​(𝕋:ℝ)|∫02​πu​𝑑x=0},u\in\mathcal{H}_{0}^{p_{0}}:=\{u\in\mathcal{H}^{p_{0}}(\mathbb{T}:\mathbb{R})|\int_{0}^{2\pi}udx=0\},

in which ℋp0\mathcal{H}^{p_{0}} is the usual Sobolev space with some p0>0p_{0}>0, the gBBM equation (3) can be rewritten as a Hamiltonian system

ut=−(1−∂x​x)−1∂x∇uH(u)\displaystyle u_{t}=-(1-\partial_{xx})^{-1}\partial_{x}\nabla_{u}H(u) (4)

with the Hamiltonian function

H⁡(u)=12​∫02​πu2​𝑑x+130​∫02​πu6​𝑑x.\displaystyle H(u)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}u^{2}dx+\frac{1}{30}\int_{0}^{2\pi}u^{6}dx. (5)

ℤ¯=ℤ∖{0},hp0:={z=(zj∈ℂ)|‖z‖p2=∑j∈ℤ¯|zj|2​j2​p0<∞}.\bar{\mathbb{Z}}=\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\},\quad h_{p_{0}}:=\{z=(z_{j}\in\mathbb{C})|\|z\|_{p}^{2}=\sum\limits_{j\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}}|z_{j}|^{2}j^{2p_{0}}<\infty\}.

u=∑j∈ℤ¯δj​zj​ϕj,ϕj=12​π​ei​j​x,δj=|j|1+j2.\displaystyle u=\sum\limits_{j\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}}\delta_{j}z_{j}\phi_{j},\quad\phi_{j}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{ijx},\quad\delta_{j}=\sqrt{\frac{|j|}{1+j^{2}}}. (6)

where

H⁡(z,z¯)=∑j≥1λj​zj​z−j+1120​π2​∑j1+j2+j3+j4+j5+j6=0,j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6∈ℤ¯δj1​δj2​δj3​δj4​δj5​δj6​zj1​zj2​zj3​zj4​zj5​zj6:=Λ+G,\displaystyle\begin{split}H(z,\bar{z})&=\sum\limits_{j\geq 1}\lambda_{j}z_{j}z_{-j}+\frac{1}{120\pi^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j_{1}+j_{2}+j_{3}+j_{4}+j_{5}+j_{6}=0,\\ j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6}\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}\end{subarray}}\delta_{j_{1}}\delta_{j_{2}}\delta_{j_{3}}\delta_{j_{4}}\delta_{j_{5}}\delta_{j_{6}}z_{j_{1}}z_{j_{2}}z_{j_{3}}z_{j_{4}}z_{j_{5}}z_{j_{6}}\\ &:=\Lambda+G,\end{split} (8)

3 Partial Birkhoff normal form

We shall use the new KAM theorem in [6] to get our desired results, so one has to extract parameters from the six order resonant terms. At the same time, we hope to remove all the six order nonresonant terms to make the perturbation small enough. However, it is difficult to reach. In [33], the authors just kill a part of the nonresonant terms with order 6 and obtain a partial Birkhoff normal form. While in [32], the authors have to eliminate some nonresonant terms of order 10 so as to avoid all the parameters being excluded. However, here we need to derive a partial Birkhoff normal form of order 14 to apply the new KAM theorem.

3.1 Normal form of order six

Let S:={±n1,±n2|1≪n1≪n2}.S:=\{\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}|~1\ll n_{1}\ll n_{2}\}. Split z=(zj)j∈ℤ¯=(z~,z^)z=(z_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{\bar{Z}}}=(\tilde{z},\hat{z}) with z~=(zn1,zn2,z−n1,z−n2)\tilde{z}=(z_{n_{1}},z_{n_{2}},z_{-n_{1}},z_{-n_{2}}). We define the index sets Δ∗\Delta_{*}(*=0,1,2) and Δ3\Delta_{3} as follows:

Δ∗={(j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6)∈ℤ¯6| There are just * components of j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6 not in S},\displaystyle\begin{split}\Delta_{*}&=\{(j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{6}|\text{ There are just * components of }\\ &\qquad j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6}\text{ not in S}\},\\ \end{split}
Δ3={(j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6)∈ℤ¯6| There exist at least 3 components ofj1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6 not in S}.\displaystyle\begin{split}\Delta_{3}&=\{(j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{6}|\text{ There exist at least 3 components of}\\ &\qquad j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6}\text{ not in S}\}.\end{split}

We also define the normal formal set in the following form

𝒩:={(j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6)∈ℤ¯6|(j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6)≡(a,−a,b,−b,c,−c)},\mathcal{N}:=\{(j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{6}|(j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6})\equiv(a,-a,b,-b,c,-c)\},

in which (j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6)=(a,−a,b,−b,c,−c)(j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6})=(a,-a,b,-b,c,-c) or its possible permutations. Let us split GG into three parts, one has

G=G¯+G~+G^,\displaystyle G=\bar{G}+\tilde{G}+\hat{G}, (14)

+32​π2​[n12​n2(1+n12)2​(1+n22)​|zn1|4​|zn2|2+n1​n22(1+n12)​(1+n22)2​|zn1|2​|zn2|4]+32​π2∑j≥1​ and ​j≠n1,n2j1+j2[n12(1+n12)2|zn1|4|+n22(1+n22)2|zn2|4]|zj|2+6π2∑j≥1​ and ​j≠n1,n2n1​n2​j(1+n12)​(1+n22)​(1+j2)|zn1|2|zn2|2|zj|2.\displaystyle\begin{split}&+\frac{3}{2\pi^{2}}\biggl[\frac{n_{1}^{2}n_{2}}{(1+n_{1}^{2})^{2}(1+n_{2}^{2})}|z_{n_{1}}|^{4}|z_{n_{2}}|^{2}+\frac{n_{1}n_{2}^{2}}{(1+n_{1}^{2})(1+n_{2}^{2})^{2}}|z_{n_{1}}|^{2}|z_{n_{2}}|^{4}\biggr]\\ &+\frac{3}{2\pi^{2}}\sum\limits_{j\geq 1\text{ and }j\neq n_{1},n_{2}}\frac{j}{1+j^{2}}\biggl[\frac{n_{1}^{2}}{(1+n_{1}^{2})^{2}}|z_{n_{1}}|^{4}|+\frac{n_{2}^{2}}{(1+n_{2}^{2})^{2}}|z_{n_{2}}|^{4}\biggr]|z_{j}|^{2}\\ &+\frac{6}{\pi^{2}}\sum\limits_{j\geq 1\text{ and }j\neq n_{1},n_{2}}\frac{n_{1}n_{2}j}{(1+n_{1}^{2})(1+n_{2}^{2})(1+j^{2})}|z_{n_{1}}|^{2}|z_{n_{2}}|^{2}|z_{j}|^{2}.\end{split}

(17)

To remove the part G~\tilde{G}, We need the following proposition.

Proposition 3.1.

For each (j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6)∈(Δ0∪Δ1∪Δ2)∖𝒩(j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4},j_{5},j_{6})\in(\Delta_{0}\cup\Delta_{1}\cup\Delta_{2})\setminus\mathcal{N}, one has

where C⁡(n1,n2)>0C(n_{1},n_{2})>0 is a constant depending only on n1n_{1} and n2n_{2}.

Proof.

We shall discuss the proposition into several cases.

Case(I). When j5+j6=0j_{5}+j_{6}=0.

|λj1+λj2+λj3+λj4+λj5+λj6|=|λj1+λj2+λj3+λj4|.|\lambda_{j_{1}}+\lambda_{j_{2}}+\lambda_{j_{3}}+\lambda_{j_{4}}+\lambda_{j_{5}}+\lambda_{j_{6}}|=|\lambda_{j_{1}}+\lambda_{j_{2}}+\lambda_{j_{3}}+\lambda_{j_{4}}|.

Case(I-1). j5,j6∈{±n1,±n2}.j_{5},j_{6}\in\{\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}\}.

    Three components of j1,j2,j3,j4j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4} are negative, the other one is positive. Without loss of generality, we assume j1>0j_{1}>0 and j2,j3,j4<0j_{2},j_{3},j_{4}<0.

  • •

    Two components of j1,j2,j3,j4j_{1},j_{2},j_{3},j_{4} are negative, while the remaining ones are positive. Without loss of generality, one assumes that j1,j4>0,j2,j3<0j_{1},j_{4}>0,j_{2},j_{3}<0 and j1≤|j2|≤|j3|≤j4.j_{1}\leq|j_{2}|\leq|j_{3}|\leq j_{4}.

    It is easily check that the function f⁡(t)=t1+t2f(t)=\frac{t}{1+t^{2}} is convex for t≥2.t\geq 2. Then we shall discuss it into two subcases. On one hand, when j1≥2,j_{1}\geq 2, it follows that

    |λj1+λj2+λj3+λj4|=|f⁡(j1)+f⁡(j4)−f⁡(|j2|)−f⁡(|j3|)|=|f⁡(j1)−f⁡(|j2|)−(f⁡(|j3|)−f⁡(j4))|≥|f⁡(j1)−f⁡(|j2|)−(f⁡(|j2|)−f⁡(j4+|j3|−|j2|))|=|f⁡(j1)−2​f​(|j2|)+f⁡(2​|j2|−j1)|≥|f′′​(2​n2)|:=C⁡(n1,n2),\displaystyle\begin{split}&|\lambda_{j_{1}}+\lambda_{j_{2}}+\lambda_{j_{3}}+\lambda_{j_{4}}|\\ =&|f(j_{1})+f(j_{4})-f(|j_{2}|)-f(|j_{3}|)|\\ =&|f(j_{1})-f(|j_{2}|)-(f(|j_{3}|)-f(j_{4}))|\\ \geq&|f(j_{1})-f(|j_{2}|)-(f(|j_{2}|)-f(j_{4}+|j_{3}|-|j_{2}|))|\\ =&|f(j_{1})-2f(|j_{2}|)+f(2|j_{2}|-j_{1})|\\ \geq&|f^{\prime\prime}(2n_{2})|:=C(n_{1},n_{2}),\end{split} (20)

    the last inequality follows from the fact that j1≤n2.j_{1}\leq n_{2}.

    On the other hand, if j1=1j_{1}=1, one has 1+j4=|j2|+|j3|.1+j_{4}=|j_{2}|+|j_{3}|. Notice that at least two components of j2,j3,j4j_{2},j_{3},j_{4} lie in S,S, it deduces that |j2|,|j3|,j4≥n1|j_{2}|,|j_{3}|,j_{4}\geq n_{1}. Thus,

    |λj1+λj2+λj3+λj4|=12+O⁡(1n1)≥14.|\lambda_{j_{1}}+\lambda_{j_{2}}+\lambda_{j_{3}}+\lambda_{j_{4}}|=\frac{1}{2}+O(\frac{1}{n_{1}})\geq\frac{1}{4}. (21)

Case(I-2). j5,j6∉{±n1,±n2}.j_{5},j_{6}\notin\{\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}\}.

This case is trivial.

Case (II). When j5+j6≠0.j_{5}+j_{6}\neq 0.

    At this time, j1+j2+j3+j4+j5+j6=r​n1−(6−r)​n2=0,j_{1}+j_{2}+j_{3}+j_{4}+j_{5}+j_{6}=rn_{1}-(6-r)n_{2}=0, where 1≤r≤5.1\leq r\leq 5. Thus

Based on the proposition 3.1, we obtain the following partial Birkhoff normal form proposition.

with the coefficients

It follows from the Proposition 1.1 that λj1+λj2+λj3+λj4+λj5+λj6≠0\lambda_{j_{1}}+\lambda_{j_{2}}+\lambda_{j_{3}}+\lambda_{j_{4}}+\lambda_{j_{5}}+\lambda_{j_{6}}\neq 0 when j1+j2+j3+j4+j5+j6=0.j_{1}+j_{2}+j_{3}+j_{4}+j_{5}+j_{6}=0. Thus FF is well defined.

where ∗* represents the convolution operation. Secondly, using the Taylor’s formula, one has

3.2 Normal form of order ten

To obtain the partial Birkhoff normal form of order ten, one requires to define some new index sets in the following way:

𝒩′={(j1,⋯,j10)∈ℤ¯10:There exists a 10-permutation τ such thatjτ⁡(1)=−jτ⁡(2),jτ⁡(3)=−jτ⁡(4),jτ⁡(5)=−jτ⁡(6),jτ⁡(7)=−jτ⁡(8),jτ⁡(9)=−jτ⁡(10)},\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{N}^{\prime}&=\{(j_{1},\cdots,j_{10})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{10}:\text{There exists a 10-permutation $\tau$ such that}\\ &\quad j_{\tau(1)}=-j_{\tau(2)},j_{\tau(3)}=-j_{\tau(4)},j_{\tau(5)}=-j_{\tau(6)},j_{\tau(7)}=-j_{\tau(8)},j_{\tau(9)}=-j_{\tau(10)}\},\end{split}
Δ0′={(j1,⋯,j10)∈ℤ¯10:All the components of j1,⋯,j10 are in{±n1,±n2}},\displaystyle\begin{split}\Delta_{0}^{\prime}&=\{(j_{1},\cdots,j_{10})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{10}:\text{All the components of $j_{1},\cdots,j_{10}$ are in}\\ &\qquad\{\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}\}\},\end{split}
Δ1′={(j1,⋯,j10)∈ℤ¯10:There is only one component of j1,⋯,j10not in {±n1,±n2}},Δ2′={(j1,⋯,j10)∈ℤ¯10:There are at least two components of j1,⋯,j10 not in {±n1,±n2}}.\displaystyle\begin{split}\Delta_{1}^{\prime}&=\{(j_{1},\cdots,j_{10})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{10}:\text{There is only one component of $j_{1},\cdots,j_{10}$}\\ &\quad\text{not in }\{\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}\}\},\\ \Delta_{2}^{\prime}&=\{(j_{1},\cdots,j_{10})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{10}:\text{There are at least two components of $j_{1},\cdots,j_{10}$ }\\ &\qquad\text{not in }\{\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}\}\}.\end{split}

By what we have just defined, one has the following lemma.

Lemma 3.3.

Assume that n1,n2∈Sn_{1},n_{2}\in S, then for (j1,j2,⋯,j10)∈(Δ0′∪Δ1′)∖𝒩′(j_{1},j_{2},\cdots,j_{10})\in(\Delta_{0}^{\prime}\cup\Delta_{1}^{\prime})\setminus\mathcal{N}^{\prime} satisfying j1+j2+⋯+j10=0j_{1}+j_{2}+\cdots+j_{10}=0, we have

|λj1+λj2+⋯λj10|≥C(n1,n2),\displaystyle|\lambda_{j_{1}}+\lambda_{j_{2}}+\cdots\lambda_{j_{10}}|\geq C(n_{1},n_{2}),

in which C⁡(n1,n2)C(n_{1},n_{2}) denotes a positive constant depending only on n1,n2.n_{1},n_{2}.

Without loss of generality, we assume that the component j10∉{±n1,±n2}j_{10}\notin\{\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}\}. Let α,α¯,β,β¯\alpha,\bar{\alpha},\beta,\bar{\beta} be the number of n1,−n1,n2,−n2n_{1},-n_{1},n_{2},-n_{2} in {j1,j2,⋯,j9}\{j_{1},j_{2},\cdots,j_{9}\} respectively. Thus one has

(α−α¯)​n1+(β−β¯)​n2+j10=0,\displaystyle(\alpha-\bar{\alpha})n_{1}+(\beta-\bar{\beta})n_{2}+j_{10}=0, (34)

and

α+α¯+β+β¯=9.\displaystyle\alpha+\bar{\alpha}+\beta+\bar{\beta}=9. (35)

    Case 1: α≠α¯\alpha\neq\bar{\alpha} and β≠β¯.\beta\neq\bar{\beta}.
    From (34), we obtain that |j10|≥|β−β¯|2​n2.|j_{10}|\geq\frac{|\beta-\bar{\beta}|}{2}n_{2}. Therefore, one has

    |λj1+λj2+⋯+λj10|≥|α−α¯|​n11+n12−|β−β¯|​n21+n22−|j10|1+j102≥|α−α¯|2​n11+n12.\displaystyle\begin{split}|\lambda_{j_{1}}+\lambda_{j_{2}}+\cdots+\lambda_{j_{10}}|&\geq|\alpha-\bar{\alpha}|\frac{n_{1}}{1+n_{1}^{2}}-|\beta-\bar{\beta}|\frac{n_{2}}{1+n_{2}^{2}}-\frac{|j_{10}|}{1+j_{10}^{2}}\\ &\geq\frac{|\alpha-\bar{\alpha}|}{2}\frac{n_{1}}{1+n_{1}^{2}}.\end{split}

By simple calculation, the formula of (32) can be rewritten as

R={G¯+G^+12G~,F}+∫01{{(1−t)(G^+G¯+12(1−t2)G~,F},F}∘XFtdt,\displaystyle R=\{\bar{G}+\hat{G}+\frac{1}{2}\tilde{G},F\}+\int_{0}^{1}\{\{(1-t)(\hat{G}+\bar{G}+\frac{1}{2}(1-t^{2})\tilde{G},F\},F\}\circ X_{F}^{t}dt, (38)

|T|=O⁡(‖z‖p14).\displaystyle|T|=O(\|z\|_{p}^{14}). (43)

3.3 Normal form of order 14

In this subsection, we shall remove some terms of order 14 to guarantee that the perturbation satisfies the Assumption C for the KAM theorem 5.1. For this, we define the normal form set

𝒩′′={(j1,⋯,j14)∈ℤ¯14: There exists a 14-permutation τ such that jτ⁡(1)=−jτ⁡(2),jτ⁡(3)=−jτ⁡(4),jτ⁡(5)=−jτ⁡(6),jτ⁡(7)=−jτ⁡(8),jτ⁡(9)=−jτ⁡(10),jτ⁡(11)=−jτ⁡(12),jτ⁡(13)=−jτ⁡(14)},\displaystyle\begin{split}\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime}&=\{(j_{1},\cdots,j_{14})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{14}:\text{ There exists a 14-permutation $\tau$ such that }\\ &j_{\tau(1)}=-j_{\tau(2)},j_{\tau(3)}=-j_{\tau(4)},j_{\tau(5)}=-j_{\tau(6)},j_{\tau(7)}=-j_{\tau(8)},j_{\tau(9)}=-j_{\tau(10)},\\ &j_{\tau(11)}=-j_{\tau(12)},j_{\tau(13)}=-j_{\tau(14)}\},\end{split}

and the index sets as follows:

Δ0′′={(j1,⋯,j14)∈ℤ¯14:All the components are in ​{±n1,±n2}},\displaystyle\Delta_{0}^{\prime\prime}=\{(j_{1},\cdots,j_{14})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{14}:\text{All the components are in }\{\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}\}\},
Δ1′′={(j1,⋯,j14)∈ℤ¯14:∃ at least one component not in ​{±n1,±n2}}.\displaystyle\Delta_{1}^{\prime\prime}=\{(j_{1},\cdots,j_{14})\in\bar{\mathbb{Z}}^{14}:\exists\text{ at least one component not in }\{\pm n_{1},\pm n_{2}\}\}.

By direct computation, the expression of TT in proposition 3.4 reads

T={{12​(G¯+G^)+13​G~,F},F}+∫01{{{12(t−1)2(G¯+G^)+16(t3−3t+2)G~,F},F},F}∘XFtdt,\displaystyle\begin{split}T&=\{\{\frac{1}{2}(\bar{G}+\hat{G})+\frac{1}{3}\tilde{G},F\},F\}\\ &+\int_{0}^{1}\{\{\{\frac{1}{2}(t-1)^{2}(\bar{G}+\hat{G})+\frac{1}{6}(t^{3}-3t+2)\tilde{G},F\},F\},F\}\circ X_{F}^{t}dt,\\ \end{split} (44)

where the order of the first term is 14, and the order of the second term is at least 18.

{{12​(G¯+G^)+13​G~,F},F}=T¯+T~+T^,\displaystyle\{\{\frac{1}{2}(\bar{G}+\hat{G})+\frac{1}{3}\tilde{G},F\},F\}=\bar{T}+\tilde{T}+\hat{T}, (45)

To this end, it requires to establish a lemma about the divisor λj1+⋯λj14\lambda_{j_{1}}+\cdots\lambda_{j_{14}}:

Suppose n1≪n2,n_{1}\ll n_{2}, then for (j1,⋯,j14)∈Δ0′′∖𝒩′′(j_{1},\cdots,j_{14})\in\Delta_{0}^{\prime\prime}\setminus\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} fulfilling j1+⋯+j14=0,j_{1}+\cdots+j_{14}=0, one has

5 Appendix

5.1 KAM theorem with normal frequencies of finite limit-point

In this appendix, we shall present the new KAM theorem with normal formal frequencies of finite limit-point developed by the third author [6]. To this end, we shall introduce some notations. We start with an infinite dimensional Hamiltonian in the form of an integrable parameter dependent normal form part NN plus a Hamiltonian perturbation PP

𝒯0n:=𝕋n×{y=0}×{z=0}×{z¯=0}.\mathcal{T}_{0}^{n}:=\mathbb{T}^{n}\times\{y=0\}\times\{z=0\}\times\{\bar{z}=0\}.

Assumption A

:(Non-degeneracy.) Suppose that ω0​(ξ):𝒪⊂ℝn→ℤn\omega^{0}(\xi):\mathcal{O}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{Z}^{n} is real continuously differentiable in ξ∈𝒪\xi\in\mathcal{O} in the sense of Whitney. Suppose there exist two positive constants c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} fulfilling

infξ∈𝒪|det∂ξω0​(ξ)|≥c1,supξ∈𝒪|det∂ξω0​(ξ)|≤c2.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\inf\limits_{\xi\in\mathcal{O}}|\det\partial_{\xi}\omega^{0}(\xi)|\geq c_{1},\\ &\sup\limits_{\xi\in\mathcal{O}}|\det\partial_{\xi}\omega^{0}(\xi)|\leq c_{2}.\\ \end{split} (70)
